tiles.alt: CHAPTER THREE / The Boy Who Lived
A wall calendar for August 1991, every day crossed off in red up to the 29th, which is circled: "D.A.!" / Thirty days is a very long time to wait, when you've just found out that magic is real.
3 a.m. / practising / Harry: Wingardium… Leviosa.

A busy London street of bookshops. Between them, a grubby little pub called the Leaky Cauldron that no passer-by so much as glances at. / London. The twenty-ninth of August. / Harry: Nobody's even looking at it. / McGonagall: They can't see it.

Inside the Leaky Cauldron: dim, wood-beamed, smoky. Witches and wizards at small tables, an old barman behind the bar, and in the far corner by the fire, a pale young man. / It was dark, and shabby, and full of people in pointed hats.
Tom: Good Lord. Is this—can this be…?
A question like that deserved his very best. / Harry: Am I—could I be—maybe—you never know—if I'm not—but then the question is… / Harry: Who?
Tom: Bless my soul. Harry Potter… what an honour.
Harry: Well, yes, you're quite perceptive, most people don't realise it so quickly— / McGonagall: That's enough. Don't pester the boy, Tom. He's new to all this.
Doris: But it is him? It's Harry Potter? / Doris: I only want to shake his hand.

Close on two hands: an old woman's, wrinkled, clasping Harry's small one. A tear falls onto them. / Doris: My grandson was an Auror. Died in seventy-nine. / Doris: Thank you, Harry Potter. Thank heavens for you.
Harry: You're… welcome? / He turned his head and shot Professor McGonagall a frightened, pleading look.
Chairs scraped. The whole room was rising.
McGonagall stamps her foot; the sound is enormous; everyone freezes. / Professor McGonagall slammed her foot down. It gave Harry a new referent for the phrase "Crack of Doom".
McGonagall: We're in a hurry. / …in a voice that sounded perfectly, utterly normal.

In the corner by the fire, a pale, thin, balding young man with a twitching eye watches Harry. The panel seems subtly wrong, its colours split. / In the corner, a pale young man with a twitching eye was watching him.
Harry's eyes meet the stranger's. A low, wrong hum. / mmmmmmmmmm
Harry: Professor? Who was that pale man, by the corner? The one with the twitching eye?
McGonagall: Hm? That was Professor Quirinus Quirrell. He'll be teaching Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts this year.
Harry: I had the strangest feeling that I knew him. / Harry: And that I shouldn't shake his hand.
McGonagall: Mr Potter… how much have you been told… about how your parents died?
Harry: My parents are alive and well. They always refused to talk about how my genetic parents died. / Harry: From which I infer that it wasn't good.
McGonagall: An admirable loyalty. Though it hurts a little, to hear you say it like that. / McGonagall: Lily and James were friends of mine.
Harry: I'm sorry. But I have a Mum and Dad. / Harry: And I'd just make myself unhappy, comparing that reality to… something perfect I built up in my imagination.
McGonagall: That is amazingly wise of you. / McGonagall: But your parents died very well indeed, Mr Potter. Protecting you.
Harry: Protecting me?
McGonagall: Something of a disguise. So that doesn't happen again. Not until you're ready.
McGonagall taps a brick three times with her wand. / tap / tap / tap
The brick hollowed. / It dilated, and shivered…

Diagon Alley: a winding street of crooked, tall, brightly-painted shops, bunting overhead, crowds in robes and pointed hats. Harry and McGonagall stand at the entrance. / …into a huge archway. / And they walked forwards, together, into the wizarding world.
Harry didn't blink. It wasn't like anyone was turning into a cat.
merch: "Made with real Flubber!" / ?: Spoons with a +4 bonus!

Harry's head kept rotating, like it was trying to wind itself off his neck. / Harry: It's like the magic items section of a Dungeons & Dragons rulebook! What if one of these is one of the three you need to complete the cycle of infinite wish spells?!
Harry had veered off, entirely without thinking, toward a shop with fiery letters in the window. / McGonagall: Mr Potter?
Harry: I'm sorry! When you walk past a bookshop you haven't visited before, you have to go in and look around. / Harry: It's the family rule.
McGonagall: That is the most Ravenclaw thing I have ever heard.
Harry: What? / McGonagall: Nothing.
Harry: Don't get me wrong, this is a great distraction. Probably the best distraction anyone has ever tried on me. / Harry: But don't think I've forgotten about our pending discussion.
McGonagall: I suppose it would be rather pointless to hide it, when anyone on the street could tell you. / McGonagall: Very well.
Shadow-theatre: a tall hooded silhouette with two red slits for eyes against a sick green sky. / And she told him of the Dark Lord.

Harry whispers the name, and the panel freezes over. / Harry: Voldemort? / Harry: The name burned with a cold feeling. Ruthlessness. Diamond clarity. A hammer of titanium descending on an anvil of flesh.
Harry: He resolved, then and there, to use safer terms. Like You-Know-Who.

Shadow-theatre: the Dark Lord towers, arms raised, over cowering figures. / He raged upon wizarding Britain like a wilding wolf. Other countries wrung their hands, and hesitated. Whoever was first to oppose him would be his next target. / bystander effect!
Five masked figures in a row, their pale masks the only light in them. / The Death Eaters followed in his wake. They wielded more than wands: wealth, and power, and secrets held in blackmail.

An empty newsroom. A single newspaper, "ENOUGH!" by Yermy Wibble, is nailed to the wall. / A journalist named Yermy Wibble called for everyone to stand together. It was absurd, he wrote, for the many to cower in fear of the few. / The next morning, they found what was left of him, his wife, and his two daughters, nailed to the newsroom wall.
Whoever stood out the most became the next example. / Until the names of James and Lily Potter rose to the top of that list.

Silhouettes: a young man with untidy hair and glasses, and a young woman holding a baby. / They might have died with their wands in their hands and not regretted it, for they were heroes. / But they had an infant son.
Harry: I didn't know those people. Not really. They aren't my parents now. It would be pointless to feel so sad for them.

Harry cries into McGonagall's robes. She holds him, and she is crying too. / When Harry was done sobbing into the witch's robes, he looked up, and felt a little better to see tears in Professor McGonagall's eyes as well.
Harry: So what happened?
A cottage at night in a village. Warm lamplight in the windows. / "The Dark Lord came to Godric's Hollow. You should have been hidden. But you were betrayed."
The same cottage, its windows blazing with sickly green light. / "He killed James. He killed Lily. And he came, in the end, to you. To your cot." / "He cast the Killing Curse."
"The Killing Curse is formed of pure hate. It strikes directly at the soul. It cannot be blocked, and whomever it strikes, they die." / "But you survived. You are the only person ever to survive."

A lightning-bolt scar, glowing faintly red in the dark. / "The curse rebounded, and struck the Dark Lord, leaving only the burnt hulk of his body, and a scar upon your forehead." / "That was the end of the terror. We were free. That is why people want to see your scar, and shake your hand."
? / (And somewhere in the back of his mind was a small, small note of confusion. A sense of something wrong about that story. But he was distracted.)
Harry: I'll—have to think about this.
Harry: You can call them my parents, if you want. You don't have to say "genetic parents". / Harry: I guess there's no reason I can't have two mothers and two fathers.
McGonagall, moved beyond words. / There was no sound from Professor McGonagall.

Gringotts: a vast white marble bank with columns and bronze doors. Harry and McGonagall, tiny, at the foot of its steps. / They walked together in silence, until they came before a great white building with vast bronze doors.
To be continued
